title: Crankshaft Position Sensor "A" Circuit
plain: The engine computer says there's a fault in the circuit for crankshaft position sensor A. This sensor tells the computer engine speed and piston position, so problems can cause stalling or a no-start.
symptoms: Engine stalls, often when warm, and may not restart until it cools
Stumbling, misfiring or a jumpy tachometer

causes.name: Failed crankshaft position sensor
Damaged wiring or loose, oil-soaked connector
Damaged or loose reluctor (tone) ring on the crank or flywheel
Excess gap between sensor and tone ring, or metal debris on the sensor tip
Engine computer fault

checks: Check whether the tachometer moves while cranking
Inspect the sensor's connector and wiring for oil, heat damage or chafing
Test the sensor signal with a scope or meter before replacing it
fix: Most often a new crankshaft position sensor; check the wiring first, and use a quality brand part.
examples: Nissan recalled crankshaft sensors on some early-2000s Altima and Sentra 2.5 models for stalling
drive: Be cautious: a failing crank sensor can make the engine stall without warning, even in traffic, and it may not restart until it cools. If it has stalled or stumbles, keep trips short and avoid highways until it's fixed. If it won't start, have it towed.
test_first: Check the crank sensor signal with a scope or scan tool, inspect the wiring and connector for oil or damage, and check the sensor gap and tone ring before replacing the sensor.
urgent_if: If the check engine light is flashing or the engine is shaking hard, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off. Don't keep driving; a heavy misfire can overheat and ruin the catalytic converter and leave you without power in traffic. Have it towed or checked right away.

title: Knock Sensor 4 Circuit (Bank 2)
plain: The engine computer reports a problem with the signal from knock sensor 4 on bank 2. The knock sensor listens for pinging, so the computer may retard timing to be safe, costing a little power and mileage.
symptoms: Slightly less power or sluggish acceleration
Fuel economy may drop a little

causes.name: Damaged, corroded or chafed knock sensor wiring
Failed knock sensor
Loose knock sensor or wrong mounting torque
Engine computer fault

checks: Inspect the knock sensor connector and wiring for corrosion or breaks
Check the sensor's resistance and mounting
fix: Usually a new knock sensor and/or a wiring repair.

title: Camshaft Position Sensor "A" Circuit (Bank 1 or Single Sensor)
plain: The engine computer says there's a fault in the circuit for camshaft position sensor A (bank 1 or single sensor). This sensor tracks the camshaft, which on most engines is the intake cam, so the computer can time fuel and spark.
symptoms: Stalling, rough running or reduced power

causes.name: Failed camshaft position sensor
Damaged wiring or loose, oil-soaked connector
Timing belt or chain stretched or jumped a tooth
Weak battery or charging voltage during cranking
Engine computer fault

checks: Inspect the sensor connector for oil, corrosion or a broken lock tab
Check battery and charging voltage
Compare cam and crank signals with a scan tool or scope to check timing
fix: Usually a new camshaft position sensor or a wiring repair; if the timing is off, the timing belt or chain needs attention.
drive: If it starts and runs smoothly, you can usually drive gently to a shop soon. If it stalls, runs rough or loses power, limit driving and avoid highways. If you hear rattling or the engine runs very rough, stop; a jumped timing belt or chain can cause serious engine damage.
test_first: Check the bank 1 cam sensor signal and wiring and battery voltage while cranking, and verify cam-to-crank timing before replacing the sensor; a stretched or jumped timing chain or belt can set this code.

title: Ignition Coil Primary/Secondary Circuit
plain: The engine computer found a problem in an ignition coil circuit but isn't naming a specific coil. A bad coil circuit usually causes a misfire.

causes.name: Failed ignition coil
Damaged coil wiring or connector
Problem in the shared power feed to the coils
Engine computer coil driver fault

checks: Look for misfire codes that point to a specific cylinder
Inspect coil connectors and check power at each coil
fix: Find the faulty coil or wiring and repair or replace it.
urgent_if: If the check engine light is flashing or the engine is shaking hard, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off. Don't keep driving; a heavy misfire can overheat and ruin the catalytic converter and leave you without power in traffic. Have it towed or checked right away.

title: Ignition Coil "A" Primary/Secondary Circuit
plain: The engine computer found an electrical problem with ignition coil A (on most engines, the coil for cylinder 1). That cylinder will likely misfire.
symptoms: Check engine light on, possibly flashing
Hesitation or loss of power when accelerating

causes.name: Failed ignition coil A
Damaged wiring or loose connector at the coil
Worn spark plug overloading the coil
Open or shorted coil control wire back to the computer
Engine computer coil driver fault

checks: Swap the coil with another cylinder and see if the code follows it
Inspect the connector and wiring for damage, oil or corrosion
Check power and the control signal at the coil connector
fix: Usually a new ignition coil, often with a fresh spark plug; repair the wiring if the coil tests good.
drive: If the check engine light is flashing, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off. If the light is steady and it runs only a little rough, drive gently to a shop within a few days.
test_first: Check the wiring and connector at coil A, test its control wire back to the computer, check its spark plug, and swap the coil with another to see if the fault follows before replacing parts.
urgent_if: If the check engine light is flashing or the engine is shaking hard, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off. Don't keep driving; a heavy misfire can overheat and ruin the catalytic converter and leave you without power in traffic. Have it towed or checked right away.

title: Misfire Detected - Fueling Disabled
plain: A cylinder was misfiring badly enough that the computer shut off its fuel injector to protect the catalytic converter. The engine keeps running on the other cylinders, so it will feel rough and weak.
symptoms: Rough running and noticeably less power
Other misfire codes stored with it

causes.name: Severe misfire from a failed ignition coil or spark plug
Stuck or failed fuel injector
Low compression in the affected cylinder

checks: Look for the cylinder-specific misfire code stored with it
Check the plug, coil and injector on that cylinder
fix: Repair whatever is causing the misfire (often a coil or plug); the computer turns the injector back on afterward.
urgent_if: If the check engine light is flashing or the engine is shaking hard, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off. Don't keep driving; a heavy misfire can overheat and ruin the catalytic converter and leave you without power in traffic. Have it towed or checked right away.

title: Camshaft Position Sensor "B" Circuit (Bank 1)
plain: The engine computer says there's a fault in the circuit for camshaft position sensor B (bank 1). This sensor tracks the camshaft, which on most engines is the exhaust cam, so the computer can time fuel and spark.
symptoms: Stalling, rough running or reduced power

causes.name: Failed camshaft position sensor
Damaged wiring or loose, oil-soaked connector
Timing belt or chain stretched or jumped a tooth
Weak battery or charging voltage during cranking
Engine computer fault

checks: Inspect the sensor connector for oil, corrosion or a broken lock tab
Check battery and charging voltage
Compare cam and crank signals with a scan tool or scope to check timing
fix: Usually a new camshaft position sensor or a wiring repair; if the timing is off, the timing belt or chain needs attention.
drive: If it starts and runs smoothly, you can usually drive gently to a shop soon. If it stalls, runs rough or loses power, limit driving and avoid highways. If you hear rattling or the engine runs very rough, stop; a jumped timing belt or chain can cause serious engine damage.
test_first: Check the bank 1 "B" cam sensor signal and wiring and battery voltage while cranking, and verify cam-to-crank timing before replacing the sensor; a stretched or jumped timing chain or belt can set this code.
urgent_if: If the check engine light is flashing or the engine is shaking hard, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off. Don't keep driving; a heavy misfire can overheat and ruin the catalytic converter and leave you without power in traffic. Have it towed or checked right away.

title: Timing Reference High Resolution Signal A
plain: The computer has a problem with a fine-detail timing signal, usually from the crankshaft sensor or an optical sensor in the distributor, that it uses to time spark and fuel precisely.

causes.name: Faulty crankshaft or distributor position sensor
Damaged wiring or connector in the signal circuit
Electrical interference from ignition wires routed near the sensor wiring
Engine computer fault

checks: Inspect the sensor wiring and connector, and check that ignition wires aren't touching it
Test the sensor signal with a scope
fix: Usually a new crank or distributor sensor, or a wiring repair.
